task_fidelity.evidence: The temperature/surface-state restriction and necessary-not-sufficient scope are preserved, but the response is only six metal names. The stem both states which metals tin wets and explicitly tells the learner to judge only that wetting condition. Thus selecting the already-listed wet metals requires no wetting-to-soldering physical inference; this is genuine list copying under the semantic gate, not merely a loss of written production.

redundancy.evidence: The six distinct metal names each test membership once; no pair of options is equivalent, and the other five questions concern gradients, drop shape, coalescence, bubbles and capillarity rather than this metal classification.

answer_leakage.evidence: The stem explicitly supplies the full affirmative list 'copper, silver, and brass' and the negative list 'stainless steel, aluminum, or chromium'; options a/d/f and b/c/e simply repeat those names. A learner can recover the full correct set without any surface-tension or soldering reasoning.

mathematics.independent_solution: Under the given surface/temperature conditions exactly copper, silver and brass satisfy the wetting prerequisite; no inference about all-condition solderability or successful joint formation follows. True set {a,d,f}.

option_checks.evidence: Copper is explicitly wet by tin at the stipulated temperature/surface state, hence meets the necessary wetting condition.
Chromium is explicitly not wet by tin in the given conditions, so it fails the stated prerequisite.
Stainless steel belongs to the stated nonwetting group; it does not meet this wetting prerequisite.
Silver belongs to the stated wetting group and therefore meets this necessary condition, not every condition for a joint.
Aluminum is stated to be nonwetting in this model; changing surface treatment is not authorized.
Brass is stated to be wet by molten tin here and meets the specified wetting prerequisite.

task_fidelity.evidence: Each option couples center/edge with low-to-high/high-to-low surface movement. The learner must use the given tension inequality to orient a connected-film gradient spatially; same-temperature and pure-gasoline-dominated wetted-region assumptions make that inference explicit without changing the outward-migration goal. The gasoline prohibition remains.

redundancy.evidence: The four alternatives enumerate the two independent binary distinctions exactly once. Correct flow direction alone does not decide between a and b; center alone does not decide between b and c. No other view supplies the spatial answer.

answer_leakage.evidence: The stem supplies the model and inequality, not the low-to-high law or its radial orientation. The desired outward trend is a task goal, not a stated wetting-location answer; all four pairs remain grammatically parallel.

mathematics.independent_solution: Surface traction is toward higher tension. A pure-gasoline-dominated center is lower tension than the grease-containing outer film, so center wetting favors outward surface movement. Edge wetting reverses the radial gradient. Only b has both the physical law and outward geometry.

option_checks.evidence: Low-to-high is the right surface-movement direction, but a low-tension wetted edge and high-tension center give inward, not outward, movement.
Wetting the center gives low tension inside and high tension outside; movement toward higher tension is outward as requested.
The center placement is compatible with outward motion only for low-to-high surface traction; high-to-low reverses the physical gradient response.
With a low-tension edge, the option's high-to-low movement would point outward, but that is the opposite of the stipulated surface-tension-driven law.

task_fidelity.evidence: Shape is coupled to a reason, preserving the density-matched immiscible-drop task. Positive uniform interfacial tension, detachment and static equilibrium specify the fixed-volume area minimization model. Plateau attribution and analysis-only boundary are present.

redundancy.evidence: Flattened, unrestricted, spherical and polyhedral shapes invoke different physical errors. The later mercury question involves a change between multiple drops and one drop, not an alternative answer to this equilibrium shape/reason question.

answer_leakage.evidence: Neither the shape nor the minimum-area statement appears in the stem; equal density does not by itself name a shape. The mercury view's spherical-before/after assumption is about a different stated system and supplies no fixed-volume-area proof for this density-matched drop.

mathematics.independent_solution: Density matching eliminates differential gravitational deformation, not interfacial tension. At fixed drop volume, E=gamma*A with gamma>0 is minimized by the sphere. Only c gives the shape and its energy/area reason.

option_checks.evidence: Equal oil/solution densities cancel the differential body force that would flatten the detached equilibrium drop; gravity alone does not impose horizontal flattening here.
Immiscibility and explicit positive gamma retain an interface and its area cost even when densities match; an arbitrary shape is not the minimum.
The sphere uniquely minimizes surface area for the fixed volume of this free drop and hence minimizes gamma*A.
Flat faces do not minimize the area enclosing a prescribed volume; a polyhedron has greater area than the corresponding sphere.

task_fidelity.evidence: The choice preserves isolated mass, excluded external work/other stores and equilibrated endpoints, adding explicit spherical states, constant positive sigma and heat capacity to make the energy-sign argument determinate. All alternatives couple surface energy, thermal energy and temperature; mercury handling is prohibited.

redundancy.evidence: The four triples distinguish no area change, lost energy, reversed area change and conserved conversion. No other question asks which energy store receives coalescence energy; knowing a sphere's shape is insufficient to choose the thermal outcome.

answer_leakage.evidence: The formula E_s=sigma*S and energy boundary are conditions, not an evaluated area change. The learner still has to compare total initial/final areas and apply conservation; no option label or wording directly supplies the sign.

mathematics.independent_solution: For at least two spherical drops, volume conservation R^3=sum(r_i^3) gives A_final=4*pi*(sum(r_i^3))^(2/3)<4*pi*sum(r_i^2)=A_initial. Thus delta E_s<0, delta U_thermal=-delta E_s>0 in the isolated two-store model, and positive heat capacity implies delta T>0. Only d.

option_checks.evidence: Mass/volume conservation is not area conservation: merging at least two spheres strictly reduces total area and E_s.
Its negative delta E_s with zero delta U violates conservation when no external transfer or other energy store is allowed.
The final single sphere has less, not more, total area; positive constant sigma therefore cannot give an increase in E_s or cooling in this two-store model.
A strict area decrease releases positive energy to the only other permitted store, thermal energy, and positive heat capacity makes the equilibrium temperature rise.

task_fidelity.evidence: The pressure coefficient, airflow direction and subsequent trend are one coupled theoretical prediction under the original two-interface/common-pressure/constant-tension model. The view explicitly does not claim an experiment occurred. Its omission of actually constructing and measuring the experiment must remain a recorded production loss and does not remove that written task from the lesson.

redundancy.evidence: Option a tests the one-interface coefficient, b reverses flow and endpoint, and d retains the coefficient/direction but changes the endpoint; each alternative differs in a consequential relation. No other view gives the soap-film pressure law or the flow endpoint.

answer_leakage.evidence: The two interfaces are legitimate source conditions; the 4 coefficient, small-to-large direction and failure/disappearance endpoint are not stated in the stem. Matching only a coefficient leaves three options, and matching only initial direction leaves three; complete physical judgment is required.

mathematics.independent_solution: Two interfaces give delta p=4*sigma/r, so common external pressure implies higher internal pressure in the smaller bubble. Small-to-large flow further reduces r_small and increases r_large, widening rather than erasing the pressure difference. It continues toward disappearance or failure of the model, not an equal-positive-radius endpoint. Only c.

option_checks.evidence: Its direction/trend are correct, but 2*sigma/r counts only one interface; the thin soap film contributes two and requires 4*sigma/r.
The coefficient is correct, but p_small>p_large rules out spontaneous large-to-small flow. The resulting unequal-radius trajectory does not converge to equal radii.
4*sigma/r gives small-to-large flow; shrinking the high-pressure smaller bubble and growing the low-pressure larger one maintain that direction until disappearance or model failure.
Although its coefficient and initial direction are correct, that flow separates the radii further; equal radii would give equal pressures but are not approached from these unequal starting radii.

task_fidelity.evidence: The response preserves both density-ratio derivation from 55/146 mm and the insufficiency of unspecified matching property data. Same tube, complete wetting, equilibrium and common temperature remain explicit; the stem does not silently assume equal tensions or supply invented properties.

redundancy.evidence: The algebraic alternatives differ by an inverted height ratio; the data alternatives distinguish unique numeric density from underdetermination. These are complementary parts, not duplicate statements. No other choice provides this ratio or the missing property data.

answer_leakage.evidence: The absence of supplied properties is a source condition needed to judge sufficiency. It does not itself derive rho_a/rho_w or show whether unknown quantities cancel. The learner must evaluate which physical quantities the capillary model requires; formula a is not stated in the stem.

mathematics.independent_solution: rho_i*g*h_i=2*sigma_i/r follows from complete wetting in the same tube. Dividing gives rho_a/rho_w=(sigma_a/sigma_w)*(h_w/h_a)=(sigma_a/sigma_w)*(146/55). That leaves the tension ratio and water density unspecified for a numerical rho_a, so the full true set is {a,d}.

option_checks.evidence: From rho_a*h_a/sigma_a=rho_w*h_w/sigma_w, moving the heights to the opposite side gives exactly (146/55)*(sigma_a/sigma_w).
This reverses the height ratio. With equal positive tensions as a counterfactual check, smaller rise must imply larger density; 55/146 predicts the opposite.
Changing the unspecified sigma_a/sigma_w or rho_w changes rho_a while preserving both rises; heights alone cannot fix an absolute density.
Matching sigma_a, sigma_w and rho_w suffice to evaluate the derived expression once temperature/composition are specified; the two rises without these data are underdetermining.
